For a transition \(n_{2} \rightarrow n_{1}\) in the hydrogen atom the wave number is \(\bar{\nu} = R\left(\frac{1}{n_{1}^{2}} - \frac{1}{n_{2}^{2}}\right)\).

The first (lowest energy) Balmer line is \(3 \rightarrow 2\):
\(\bar{\nu}_{Balmer} = R\left(\frac{1}{4} - \frac{1}{9}\right) = \frac{5R}{36}\).

The first Brackett line is \(5 \rightarrow 4\):
\(\bar{\nu}_{Brackett} = R\left(\frac{1}{16} - \frac{1}{25}\right) = \frac{9R}{400}\).

Ratio \(= \frac{5/36}{9/400} = \frac{2000}{324} = 6.17\).

Expressed with 5 as the first term, \(6.17 = \frac{5}{0.81}\), i.e. \(5 : 0.81\).

The Aufbau filling order is \(1s, 2s, 2p, 3s, 3p, 4s, 3d, \ldots\)

Filling \(1s^{2}2s^{2}2p^{6}3s^{2}3p^{6}\) accounts for the first 18 electrons, so the 19th electron is the first electron to enter the \(4s\) orbital.

For a \(4s\) orbital: \(n = 4\), \(l = 0\), and hence \(m = 0\). The first electron placed in an orbital is assigned \(s = +\frac{1}{2}\).

The question specifies the Aufbau principle, so the anomalous ground-state configuration \(3d^{5}4s^{1}\) of chromium is deliberately not used; on strict Aufbau order \(4s\) fills before \(3d\).

Statement I is FALSE. For an ideal gas \(C_{p} - C_{v} = R > 0\), so the heat capacity at constant pressure is always GREATER than that at constant volume. At constant pressure part of the heat supplied is spent doing expansion work, so more heat is needed to produce the same temperature rise.

Statement II is TRUE. At constant volume \(w = -p_{ext}\Delta V = 0\), so \(q_{v} = \Delta U\); the whole of the heat supplied goes into the random molecular (internal) energy and appears as a temperature rise.

Statement II is in fact the reason Statement I is wrong, so the answer is that I is false and II is true.

Count the electrons released by one mole of each species in acidic medium.

\(FeC_{2}O_{4}\): \(Fe^{2+} \rightarrow Fe^{3+}\) gives 1 electron and \(C_{2}O_{4}^{2-} \rightarrow 2CO_{2}\) gives 2 electrons, total 3.

\(Fe_{2}(C_{2}O_{4})_{3}\): iron is already \(+3\) and is not oxidised; the three oxalate ions give \(3 \times 2 = 6\) electrons.

\(FeSO_{4}\): 1 electron.

For a first order reaction \(R \rightarrow P\), the integrated rate law is \([R] = [R]_{0}e^{-k_{1}t}\).

Fraction decomposed \(= \frac{[R]_{0} - [R]}{[R]_{0}} = 1 - \frac{[R]}{[R]_{0}} = 1 - e^{-k_{1}t}\).

This is the only option that behaves correctly at the limits: it equals 0 at \(t = 0\) and tends to 1 as \(t \rightarrow \infty\). Options A and B use \(e^{+k_{1}t}\), which grows without bound, and option C gives 2 at \(t = 0\).

The anion \(A^{-}\) carries one extra electron, so the neutral atom A has \(36 - 1 = 35\) electrons, i.e. \(Z = 35\), which is bromine.

Mass number \(= \text{protons} + \text{neutrons} = 35 + 45 = 80\).

Bromine is a halogen and therefore lies in group 17.

Among the halogens, \(F_{2}\) and \(Cl_{2}\) are gases, \(Br_{2}\) is a liquid and \(I_{2}\) is a solid at room temperature, so A is a liquid.

Hence 80, group 17, liquid.

Statement I is TRUE. Oxygen normally shows a covalency of two, but it can be raised above two: it is three in \(H_{3}O^{+}\) and four in species such as basic beryllium acetate, in which the central oxygen is bonded to four beryllium atoms. The absence of d orbitals in the valence shell caps this at four. As for oxidation states, in \(SO_{2}\) oxygen is bonded to the less electronegative sulphur so it is \(-2\), while in \(OF_{2}\) it is bonded to fluorine, the only element more electronegative than oxygen, so it is \(+2\).

Statement II is TRUE and is the standard textbook explanation: the anomalous behaviour of oxygen relative to S, Se and Te arises from its very small size and high electronegativity (which also give rise to strong hydrogen bonding in \(H_{2}O\) and to oxygen's inability to expand its octet).

Both statements are true.

(A) \([Cr(H_{2}O)_{6}]^{2+}\): \(Cr^{2+}\) is \(d^{4}\), high spin \(t_{2g}^{3}e_{g}^{1}\), \(n = 4\), \(\mu = \sqrt{24} = 4.90\) - (III).

Electron withdrawing power here is the inductive (\(-I\)) effect, whose standard order is
\(-NO_{2} > -CN > -COOH > -F > -Cl > -Br > -I\).

Iodine is the least electronegative of the halogens and is the weakest withdrawer of the four groups listed. \(-COOH\) withdraws through one carbonyl oxygen. \(-CN\) withdraws more strongly because the carbon is sp hybridised (higher s character, higher effective electronegativity) and is triply bonded to nitrogen. \(-NO_{2}\) is the strongest because its nitrogen carries a formal positive charge.

Increasing order: \((D) < (B) < (A) < (C)\).

Reductive ozonolysis cuts every \(C = C\) bond and caps each half with an oxygen.

The products shown are 2 mol of \(HCHO\), 1 mol of \(OHC - CO - CHO\) and 1 mol of \(CH_{3}CO - CO - COCH_{3}\). Together these account for \(2 + 3 + 5 = 10\) carbon atoms, so X is a \(C_{10}\) hydrocarbon.

Two moles of formaldehyde mean two EXOCYCLIC \(= CH_{2}\) groups. Getting two separate ring fragments (instead of one open chain) means the ring itself is cut in two places, so X also has two ring \(C = C\) bonds. All six ring carbons are therefore sp2.

In each three-carbon fragment the MIDDLE carbonyl is the ring carbon that carried the exocyclic methylene, and the two END carbonyls are the ring carbons of the cleaved ring double bonds:

- \(OHC - CO - CHO\) has H at both ends, so those two ring carbons are unsubstituted.
- \(CH_{3}CO - CO - COCH_{3}\) has \(CH_{3}\) at both ends, so those two ring carbons each carry a methyl group.

Reassembling the ring in order gives \(CH = \) then \(C( = CH_{2})\) then \(= CH\), joined on to \(C(CH_{3}) = \) then \(C( = CH_{2})\) then \( = C(CH_{3})\), with the two ring double bonds each running between an unsubstituted CH and an adjacent methyl bearing carbon. This is exactly the ring drawn in option D: a cyclohexadiene with two exocyclic methylene groups para to each other, and the two methyl groups on the ring double bonds that flank one of those methylenes.

The other options fail: options A and B contain only ONE ring double bond, so the ring could open only into a single chain rather than two fragments (and B, with three exocyclic methylenes, would give 3 mol of \(HCHO\)). Option C carries three methyl groups (\(C_{11}\)) and on cleavage would give \(CH_{3}CO - CO - CHO\) rather than the observed \(OHC - CO - CHO\).

Finkelstein reaction: an alkyl chloride or bromide is heated with \(NaI\) in dry acetone to give the alkyl iodide (\(NaCl\) and \(NaBr\) are insoluble in acetone and precipitate, driving the exchange). So (A) matches (III).

Swarts reaction: an alkyl halide is heated with a metallic fluoride such as \(SbF_{3}\) (or \(AgF\), \(Hg_{2}F_{2}\)) to give the alkyl fluoride. So (B) matches (I).

Sandmeyer reaction: an arenediazonium salt is treated with \(Cu_{2}Cl_{2}/HCl\) (or \(Cu_{2}Br_{2}/HBr\), \(CuCN/KCN\)) to replace \(- N_{2}^{+}\) by the halide. So (C) matches (IV).

Fittig reaction: two moles of aryl halide with sodium in dry ether give the biaryl. So (D) matches (II).

Hence (A)-(III), (B)-(I), (C)-(IV), (D)-(II).

Aqueous NaOH at room temperature dissolves an organic compound only if it is acidic enough to be converted into its sodium salt, i.e. carboxylic acids (\(pK_{a} \approx 4-5\)) and phenols (\(pK_{a} \approx 10\)). Ordinary alcohols (\(pK_{a} \approx 16\)), amines, aldehydes with no acidic OH, and hydrocarbons are not.

(I) benzaldehyde - no acidic hydrogen, INSOLUBLE.
(II) naphthalen-1-ol - a phenol, forms the naphthoxide, SOLUBLE.
(III) 4-(dimethylamino)phenol - the dimethylamino group is electron releasing and weakens the acidity, but it is still a phenol and is deprotonated by NaOH, SOLUBLE.
(IV) 4-(hydroxymethyl)phenol - the benzylic OH is not acidic, but the phenolic OH is, SOLUBLE.
(V) benzoic acid - SOLUBLE as sodium benzoate.
(VI) N,N-dimethylcyclohexanamine - a base, not acidic, INSOLUBLE in NaOH.
(VII) naphthalene-1-carboxylic acid - SOLUBLE as its sodium salt.
(VIII) 1,4-di-tert-butylbenzene - a hydrocarbon, INSOLUBLE.
(IX) naphthalen-1-ylmethanol - a primary benzylic alcohol, far too weakly acidic, INSOLUBLE.

Soluble compounds: (II), (III), (IV), (V) and (VII), i.e. 5.

The structure drawn is a 1,4-linked glucosyl-glucose whose right hand ring retains a free anomeric (hemiacetal) OH, and the caption attached to it asserts that maltose is a NON-reducing sugar. Because that anomeric centre can ring-open to a free aldehyde, maltose reduces Tollens' and Fehling's reagents, so it IS a reducing sugar and the statement is wrong.

Two moles of phenol condense with phthalic anhydride in concentrated \(H_{2}SO_{4}\) to give phenolphthalein, which in its closed lactone form is colourless.

On adding NaOH the lactone ring opens and one of the rings is converted into a quinonoid ring; the resulting dianion has an extended conjugated (quinonoid) chromophore and is PINK.

With EXCESS NaOH a further hydroxide ion adds to the central sp2 carbon of that quinonoid system, turning it back into an sp3 carbinol carbon. The quinonoid ring is destroyed and the conjugation joining the two aromatic rings is broken, so the resulting trianion X absorbs outside the visible region.

Hence X is COLOURLESS. This is exactly why phenolphthalein fades on standing in strongly alkaline solution.

In the perxenate ion \(XeO_{6}^{4-}\) xenon is in the \(+8\) oxidation state and uses all eight of its valence electrons in bonding to the six oxygen atoms.

The central xenon therefore forms 6 sigma bonds and is left with NO lone pair, giving a steric number of 6, \(sp^{3}d^{2}\) hybridisation and a regular octahedral shape.

Sigma bond pairs \(= 6\), lone pairs on the central atom \(= 0\).

Total \(= 6 + 0 = 6\).

\(NH_{4}OH\) (weak base) plus \(NH_{4}Cl\) (its salt) is a basic buffer, so use
\(pOH = pK_{b} + \log\frac{[salt]}{[base]}\).

Millimoles of base \(= 5 \times 0.1 = 0.5\); millimoles of salt \(= 250 \times 0.1 = 25\). Both are present in the same final volume, so the volume cancels and
\(\frac{[salt]}{[base]} = \frac{25}{0.5} = 50\).

\(\log 50 = \log\frac{100}{2} = 2 - \log 2 = 2 - 0.30 = 1.70\).

\(pOH = 4.74 + 1.70 = 6.44\).

\(pH = 14 - 6.44 = 7.56 = 756 \times 10^{-2}\).

So the required nearest integer is 756.

Step 1 - get the moles of solute from the elevation of boiling point.
\(\Delta T_{b} = 320 - 319.5 = 0.5\ K\) and \(\Delta T_{b} = K_{b} \times m\), so the molality \(m = \frac{0.5}{0.3} = 1.667\ mol\ kg^{-1}\).
Mass of solvent \(= 40\ g = 0.040\ kg\), so moles of solute \(= 1.667 \times 0.040 = 0.0667\).

Step 2 - use the relative lowering of vapour pressure, which for a non-volatile non-electrolyte solute equals the mole fraction of the solute.
\(\frac{p^{\circ} - p}{p^{\circ}} = \frac{760 - 750}{760} = \frac{1}{76} = x_{solute}\).

\(\frac{0.0667}{0.0667 + n} = \frac{1}{76}\)
\(0.0667 + n = 76 \times 0.0667 = 5.067\)
\(n = 5.0\).
